title: Two clocks, one step size: why stiffness limits the solver and why a change of coordinates must be checked
summary: A pair of exponentials with time scales 1 and 0.01 sets the stage; an explicit solver with the wrong step then blows up; and the rest of the group asks what survives a change of variables: eigenvalues, a log transform with a floor, and a progress variable that is not a clock.

media.alt: Line chart titled one system, two very different clocks. Horizontal axis dimensionless time 0 to 4, vertical axis state over initial state from 0 to 1. A solid orange curve decays slowly (time scale 1). A dashed blue curve drops to zero almost at once (time scale 0.01). A companion chart shows explicit Euler with step 0.03 oscillating with growing amplitude.

read_the_figure.question: How fast is the fastest process in the system, and does my step size respect it even when I only care about the slow one?
read_the_figure.axes: Stiffness chart: dimensionless time 0 to 4 against state divided by initial state. Solver chart: time 0 to 0.3 against state on a symmetric log axis from -1000 to 1000. Coordinates charts: original and re-expressed coordinates (x1, x2). Log chart: positive state y on a log axis from 1e-8 to 1 against transformed state.
look_at: Stiffness: the dashed blue curve is finished by t = 0.05 while the orange one is still at 0.95. A solver that wants to follow the slow curve for 4 time units must still be stable for the fast one.

Solver chart: Euler with step 0.01 (orange) lands on zero after one step; step 0.03 (blue dashed) alternates sign and grows by a factor of 2 per step, reaching about 1000 by t = 0.3. The black curve is the exact decay.
Slide 18 diagram: before and after a change of coordinates the equilibrium eigenvalues are the same, -1 and -100. The fast clock is still there.

Coordinates chart: the same path drawn in original coordinates (jumps at the end) and in a smooth linear re-expression with different axis scales; distances and angles look different although it is one path.
Log chart: log(y) is a straight line over eight decades; log(max(y, 1e-4)) is flat below y = 1e-4, at about -9.2. The flat part carries no information and has zero slope.
Slide 30 diagram: progress c = 0.6 to a time map t(c) to a delay in seconds; a peak's location in progress is not a time measurement.
read_the_figure.proves: Stability is set by the fastest clock, not the slowest; a change of variables does not remove it; and a transform with a clamp trades range for a plateau where gradients are zero.
if_wrong: A solver step above 2 over the fast rate: the numerical solution grows although the exact one decays.
Eigenvalues that differ before and after a smooth change of coordinates: a mistake in the transform or in the Jacobian.
A clamp that sits inside the range of the data: values below it become indistinguishable.
A progress variable used as if it were time: the speed of progress is not constant.
must_check: That both time scales are stated or readable.
That the step size is on the solver chart legend.
That a transform's floor (the clamp) is labelled and below the data range.
That time-map claims state how progress is converted to seconds.

terms.meaning: A wide gap between the fastest and slowest decay rates of a system.
The inverse of a decay rate: the time for a mode to shrink by a factor e.
Decay is reproduced only if |1 + h lambda| is at most 1.
A smooth invertible change of variables changes the Jacobian at an equilibrium by a similarity, so its eigenvalues stay.
A coordinate from 0 to 1 that tracks completion of a process; converting it to time requires the rate of progress.

remember: The fastest clock sets the explicit step limit for the whole run.
Euler on y' = lambda y is stable for h at most 2/|lambda|.
A coordinate change cannot remove an eigenvalue.
A clamp turns a range into a plateau with zero gradient.
t(c) is the integral of dc over the rate of progress, not c itself.

steps.title: Two clocks
steps.note: The solid and dashed curves of the first chart. At t = 0.05 the fast one has fallen to e^(-5) = 0.007.

steps.title: Why the step 0.03 blows up and the step 0.01 does not
steps.note: The factor for h = 0.01 is exactly zero; for h = 0.03 it is -2, so the iterate alternates sign and doubles each step. After 10 steps (t = 0.3) the magnitude is 1024, as plotted.

steps.title: Eigenvalues survive a change of variables
steps.note: At an equilibrium the new Jacobian is a similarity transform of the old one. A diagonal system with -1 and -100 stays -1 and -100, as slide 18 says.

steps.title: A clamp creates a plateau
steps.note: Below epsilon the derivative is zero, so a loss on g carries no gradient about y there, as the flat dashed line shows.

steps.title: From progress to time
steps.note: Progress becomes time only through the rate of progress, which is large during ignition and small elsewhere. Reading c at a peak therefore says nothing about when the peak occurs.

worked.title: Largest stable explicit step for the fast clock
worked.problem: The fast decay rate is 100 per unit time. Find the Euler stability limit and the number of steps to reach t = 4 at that limit.
worked.answer: h = 0.02 and 200 steps, although the slow part alone would need only a handful of steps for the same accuracy.

analyze.q: Why is the orange (slow) curve irrelevant to the choice of step, even though it is the one you care about?
After the coordinate change the eigenvalues are unchanged. Name two things that did change.
analyze.hint: Scaling of axes, conditioning of the loss.

evaluate.q: A log transform with a clamp at 1e-4 is used on data that reach 1e-6. What do you tell the author?
Why is 'peak location in progress' not a timing measurement? What do you need in addition?

create: Plot the Euler amplification factor |1 + h lambda| against h for lambda = -100 and mark the three step sizes of the solver chart.
Replace the clamp by a smooth floor ln(y + epsilon) and compare the gradient at y = 1e-6.

checks.q: What two time scales does the first chart show?
checks.answer: 1 for the slow curve and 0.01 for the fast one.

checks.q: Fast rate 50. Largest stable Euler step?
Why does Euler with h = 0.03 alternate in sign?
checks.answer: Because 1 + h lambda = -2, negative: the sign flips each step, and the magnitude doubles.

checks.q: Does re-expressing the variables in new coordinates make a stiff problem easy?
checks.answer: No: the eigenvalues, hence the stiffness, are unchanged at an equilibrium; only an implicit solver or structure removes the step limit.

checks.q: Design a figure that would let a reader choose a step size for a given pair of time scales.
checks.answer: A plot of the stability factor against step size on log axes, with a vertical line at 2/|lambda_fast| and the step counts marked.
